name: Xcel Energy Inc.
employees: 11,534 full-time employees at December 31, 2025, of whom approximately 44 percent (5,036) were covered by collective bargaining agreements (FY2025 Form 10-K)
summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Xcel Energy is the utility whose data-center opportunity and whose largest liability arrived in the same decade, and it is financing both out of one $60B five-year plan that carries about $5B of wildfire mitigation inside it. It has approximately 2 GW of data-center load contracted or under construction against more than 20 GW of additional pipeline, one named customer — Google, at Pine Island, Minnesota, under a 1,900 MW clean-energy package including a 300 MW / 30 GWh iron-air battery — and, on the other side of the ledger, roughly $640M paid to settle the 2021 Marshall Fire with none of it from customers, plus a Texas Panhandle fire its own regulator's forest service attributed to its poles, on which about $404M of settlements have been reached against insurance that is nearly exhausted. BACKGROUND. Minneapolis; NASDAQ: XEL. Per the FY2025 Form 10-K the company serves 3.9 million electric and 2.2 million natural gas customers across eight states through four operating companies — Northern States Power Minnesota, Northern States Power Wisconsin, Public Service Company of Colorado and Southwestern Public Service — owns 20,800 MW of generation, operates 115,000 conductor-miles of electric transmission and 225,000 of distribution, holds $81.4B of assets, employs 11,534 and reported 2025 revenue of $14,669M with ongoing earnings of $3.80 per share; 2026 guidance of $4.04–$4.16 has been reaffirmed six times and never revised. The three operating regions sit in three different market structures: the Minnesota and Wisconsin companies are in MISO, Southwestern Public Service is in SPP, and the Colorado company belongs to no regional transmission organization at all. Collection gap: Xcel names only one data-center customer and redacts the fifth row of its own pipeline slide; no supplier is named on any storage project except the Form Energy system inside the Google package, and the company states the omission is deliberate — 'additional strategic partnerships across supply chain in place but disclosure limited due to confidentiality'; no Colorado wildfire-liability statute exists in its own account of which states passed legislation; and the Q3 2026 earnings date was unposted by the company, with trackers disagreeing.
ecosystemRole: We assess Xcel as the utility in this file where the wildfire question and the load-growth question are the same balance-sheet question — and as the one that has responded by contracting its supply chain rather than its customers. Basis: about $5B of the $60B base capital plan is wildfire mitigation, a planned 2029 Colorado securitization is already embedded in the plan's own capital tables, and excess liability insurance costs about $135M a year for $450M of coverage after the market repriced; against that, the company signed two named framework agreements in the same week of February 2026 — a strategic alliance with GE Vernova reserving five F-class gas turbines and multiple gigawatts of wind turbines, and a memorandum of understanding with a NextEra Energy subsidiary to co-develop generation for large loads — and closed a 1,900 MW clean-energy package for a single Google campus. For the sellers in this corpus it is four counterparties. For turbine makers, a buyer that has converted volume into reserved manufacturing slots, at 12 gas combustion-turbine reservations with options into the 2030s. For long-duration storage, the most consequential single order in the corpus: 300 MW and 30 GWh of iron-air, procured not through a resource plan but inside a hyperscaler's service agreement. For lithium-ion storage sellers, roughly 2,200 MW of storage in the base plan with exactly one supplier named anywhere and a 300 MW four-hour company-owned battery in Minnesota whose vendor is not disclosed. And for the hyperscalers and developers here — Google by name from the company, and Meta, QTS and Aligned Data Centers from the Edison Electric Institute's project list — it is the utility whose Minnesota tariff is already approved at a 75 percent minimum demand charge over fifteen years, and whose Colorado version, filed at a 50 MW threshold and 80 percent, will be decided in early 2027.

productsAndServices.name: Regulated electric service — four operating companies, eight states, three market structures
productsAndServices.description: Xcel serves 3.9 million electric customers across Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, New Mexico and Texas through four regulated operating companies: Northern States Power Minnesota (serving Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota), Northern States Power Wisconsin (Wisconsin and Michigan), Public Service Company of Colorado, and Southwestern Public Service (Texas and New Mexico). The Minnesota and Wisconsin companies are managed together as the NSP System. What distinguishes the structure from the other utilities in this file is the wholesale layer: the NSP companies are MISO members, Southwestern Public Service is in SPP, and Public Service Company of Colorado is, in the Form 10-K's words, 'not presently a member of an RTO' — it sells into other regional markets and participates in SPP's Western Energy Imbalance Service, but no regional operator runs its capacity or plans its transmission. FY2025 rate base was approximately $56B, weighted Colorado 43 percent, Minnesota 35 percent, Southwestern Public Service 16 percent and Wisconsin 6 percent.
highlights: FY2025 electric revenue $12,160M on electric sales volume of 109,401 million kWh; 2025 peak demand was 8,445 MW on the NSP System (July 15), 7,010 MW at Public Service Company of Colorado (July 28) and 4,519 MW at Southwestern Public Service (August 8)

Weather-normalized retail electric sales for the first half of 2026 rose 2.1 percent system-wide, with commercial and industrial up 3.0 percent — driven by Southwestern Public Service at 6.2 percent and Minnesota at 2.4 percent, which the company attributes to the energy sector in Texas and New Mexico and to manufacturing across all jurisdictions

Trailing-twelve-month ongoing return on equity at June 30, 2026 was 10.96 percent at the parent but only 8.43 percent across the operating companies — Minnesota 9.59 percent, Wisconsin 10.31 percent, Southwestern Public Service 8.51 percent and Colorado 7.22 percent, the lowest in the group and the reason Colorado's rate case mattered

The Colorado Public Utilities Commission's August 2026 decision cut the electric increase to $157M, 4.4 percent, from the $225M the parties had settled, on a 9.3 percent return and a 13-month average historical test year, with rates effective August 29, 2026

Other 2026 rate outcomes: Minnesota electric approximately $211M over two years at a 9.60 percent return, up from 9.25 percent; a Southwestern Public Service New Mexico stipulation at $90M and 9.5 percent; and a Colorado gas settlement at $123M and 9.2 percent
productsAndServices.positioning: The only major utility in this file with an operating company outside any regional transmission organization, and the only one whose regulatory footprint spans eight states with four commissions plus North Dakota, South Dakota and Michigan. Against AEP, which is in three RTOs, Xcel is in two and a half — and the Colorado company's absence from an RTO means no capacity auction sets a price there and no regional planner allocates its transmission cost.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct regulated retail service under each state commission's tariffs, with capital riders and trackers between rate cases.
targetSegments: Residential and commercial customers across eight states
Industrial customers, notably the energy sector in the Texas and New Mexico panhandle territory
Hyperscale and colocation data centers under the large-load tariffs
productsAndServices.roadmap: Colorado large-load tariff decision expected early 2027; Wisconsin large-load tariff decision early 2027; the Colorado gas rate case decision expected in Q4 2026; the New Mexico decision in Q4 2026 with rates in December 2026.

productsAndServices.name: Large-load and data-center service — the three-state tariff programme and the Google agreement
productsAndServices.description: Xcel reports its data-center position in three explicit tiers and does not merge them: approximately 2 GW contracted or under construction, approximately 4 GW contracted by year-end 2027, and more than 20 GW of additional pipeline. The supporting terms it states are 15-year-plus contracts, individual projects of 200 MW to more than 1 GW, online dates from 2027 to beyond 2030 with ramps running through the mid-2030s, and an expectation of about 1 GW signed in 2026 and about 3 GW more by the end of 2027. The commercial instrument is a large-load tariff filed in three states on a common template. Minnesota's is approved; Colorado's and Wisconsin's were filed in April and June 2026 with decisions expected in early 2027. Only one customer is named by the company: Google.
highlights: Minnesota tariff (Proceeding E-002/M-25-289), approved: applies to 100 MW and above, 15-year minimum term, 75 percent minimum demand charge, biannual five-year forecast updates, an incremental cost test, credit requirements, 12 months' notice for a capacity reduction and 24 for termination, and an exit fee of the minimum bill multiplied by the lesser of the remaining term or ten years

Colorado tariff (Proceeding 26AL-0137E), filed April 2026: a 50 MW threshold — the lowest of the three — with an 80 percent minimum demand charge and 24 months' notice for either a reduction or a termination
Wisconsin tariff (Proceeding 4220-TE-119), filed June 2026: 100 MW, 15 years, 75 percent, on the same exit-fee formula

The Google agreement at Pine Island, Minnesota: an electric service agreement under which, per the Form 10-K, 'Google will pay all costs for its new service for the duration of the contract, in accordance with Minnesota's regulatory and legislative requirements for large loads', expected to produce approximately $1.1B of benefits to Minnesota customers, filed for approval in April 2026 with a decision expected in early 2027

The package behind it: 1,900 MW of new clean energy — 1,400 MW of wind, 200 MW of solar and 300 MW of long-duration storage delivered as a 300 MW, 30 GWh Form Energy iron-air battery system — plus $50M toward the company's Capacity*Connect programme, sought through a proposed Clean Energy Accelerator Charge; approvals for 1,000 MW of the resources were pending inside existing acquisition processes as of July 2026

The company's own sizing rule for the opportunity: '1 GW data center, assuming balance of renewable, storage and natural gas generation, could require $6-8 billion of investment (including third-party generation)'

No large-load tariff exists for Southwestern Public Service in Texas or New Mexico, and Xcel does not mention Texas SB 6 anywhere in its own materials — that statute governs ERCOT, and Southwestern Public Service is an SPP participant
productsAndServices.positioning: The most conservative tier disclosure of the four utilities in this file — Xcel publishes a contracted figure roughly a tenth the size of its pipeline and redacts one of its own five project rows — and the only one whose flagship agreement is structured as a clean-energy package rather than as gas capacity. Against Entergy's sealed single-customer certificates and AEP's 69 GW of contracted load, Xcel's ~2 GW is small; against the Colorado tariff's 50 MW threshold, it is also the widest net.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Negotiated electric service agreements filed for commission approval, under state large-load tariffs where approved.
targetSegments: Hyperscalers and large developers, per the company's own slide
Colocation operators, with QTS in Aurora, Colorado and Aligned Data Centers in Abernathy, Texas named on the Edison Electric Institute's project list
Industrial loads in the Panhandle energy sector
productsAndServices.roadmap: Approximately 1 GW expected to be signed during 2026 and about 3 GW more by the end of 2027; Colorado and Wisconsin tariff decisions in early 2027; the Google service agreement and its Clean Energy Accelerator Charge decided in early 2027.

productsAndServices.name: Generation — 20,800 MW owned, the coal exit, and the build behind the load
productsAndServices.description: Xcel owns 20,800 MW of generating capacity and states it has reduced carbon emissions from generation serving customers by an estimated 58 percent from 2005 levels while remaining on track to exit coal entirely by the end of 2030 — Comanche Unit 3 in Colorado carries a published 2030 retirement year. Its wind capacity is approximately 11,000 MW including nearly 4,500 MW owned. The 2026–2030 base capital plan adds approximately 11,400 MW of renewable generation, 3,400 MW of natural gas and 2,200 MW of energy storage; the incremental plan would add 2,000 MW of wind, 1,900 MW of solar, 400 MW of gas and 300 MW of storage on top. The build is unevenly distributed in time: Colorado front-loads, with 1,585 MW entering service in 2026 and nothing after 2028, while Southwestern Public Service back-loads hard, at roughly 2,490 MW in 2028 and 1,740 MW across 2029 and 2030.
highlights: Minnesota: the Upper Midwest Resource Plan settlement approved by the commission in February 2025 selected a company-owned 420 MW Lyon County combustion turbine and a company-owned 300 MW four-hour Sherco battery, plus 3,200 MW of wind, 400 MW of solar and 600 MW of storage through 2030, and extended the nuclear units' lives into the early 2050s — the Monticello plant received federal approval in January 2025 to operate to 2050

Colorado: the 2024 Electric Resource Plan's Phase I was approved in November 2025 on a load forecast of 3 percent compound annual sales growth through 2031 and a capacity need of approximately 5,400 MW; the Phase II competitive solicitation had not been run as of mid-2026, so no Phase II winners exist. What Colorado awarded in February 2026 was the separate Near-Term Procurement — 3,200 MW approved immediately across ten projects, including a 200 MW company-owned gas combustion turbine, with 600 to 1,500 MW of company-owned wind, solar and storage conditionally approved

Southwestern Public Service: a July 2025 portfolio of 17 new projects totalling 5,168 MW nameplate by 2030 (3,121 MW accredited) — 1,273 MW of wind, 695 MW of solar, 1,112 MW of storage and 2,088 MW of gas — plus 521 MW of life extensions at Nichols, Maddox and Plant X; the company puts its projected resource need at 5,300 to 10,200 MW of nameplate capacity by 2030

Coal conversions rather than pure retirements where the site is useful: Pawnee in Colorado retired in 2025 and completed conversion to natural gas in 2026; the Harrington plant in Amarillo converted three units to gas across 2024–2025 at 1,018 MW; Wisconsin retired four combustion turbines in 2025 and replaced them with one 206 MW turbine and five reciprocating units

The only storage supplier Xcel names anywhere is Form Energy, for the 300 MW / 30 GWh iron-air system inside the Google package — a 100-hour duration implied by the ratio, and by the trade press's account the largest battery project by energy capacity announced anywhere to date. No supplier is named for the company-owned 300 MW four-hour Sherco battery or for any other storage in the plan
productsAndServices.positioning: A buyer that has moved its supply-chain risk upstream into reservation agreements rather than project-by-project procurement, and the only utility in this file with a utility-scale long-duration storage order. Its storage volume — about 2,200 MW in the base plan — is the largest of the four utilities here, and its supplier disclosure is the thinnest.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Company-owned self-builds and power purchase agreements selected through state resource-plan solicitations, plus direct multi-year equipment reservation agreements with manufacturers.
targetSegments: Its own four operating companies' native load
Large-load customers whose service agreements underwrite specific resources, as in the Clean Energy Accelerator Charge structure
productsAndServices.roadmap: Base-plan generation entering service at approximately 2,100 MW in 2026, 2,640 MW in 2027, 3,815 MW in 2028 and 2,840 MW across 2029–2030; Colorado's Phase II RFP was due in the third quarter of 2026; a Southwestern Public Service recommendation for approximately 2,600 MW of company-owned generation and a Minnesota RFP for approximately 4,100 MW of renewables and storage by 2030 sit in the incremental plan.

productsAndServices.name: Transmission — 115,000 conductor-miles, and the 765 kV question in SPP
productsAndServices.description: Electric transmission carries $15,440M of the 2026–2030 base capital plan, the largest single functional line, against 115,000 conductor-miles in service. The regional context differs by company: the NSP companies build inside MISO's long-range plans, Southwestern Public Service inside SPP's Integrated Transmission Plan, and Public Service Company of Colorado outside any regional planning process. Xcel was selected in February 2025 to construct the first 765 kV lines within SPP, and a further Crawfish Draw to Phantom 765 kV line at approximately $2B sits in the company's stated line-of-sight capital alongside additional 765 kV lines from the 2025 SPP portfolio, which are competitively bid.
highlights: Named MISO projects: the long-range transmission plan's 'Grid Forward' and 'Western Wisconsin Transmission Connection'; MISO Tranche 2.2, dated 2030 and beyond, sits in the incremental plan rather than the base

The base capital forecast explicitly excludes 'additional generation investment associated with resource plans and SPP and MISO Tranche 2 transmission projects' — so the transmission line in the plan understates the company's own view of the opportunity
Approximately 1,700 new transmission line miles are in the 2026–2030 plan
Xcel is one of the Grid North Partners in MISO's Tranche 2.1 portfolio, per the consortium's other members

The Colorado Transmission Cost Adjustment recovers, between rate cases, transmission projects that increase capacity or that form part of an approved wildfire mitigation plan — a mechanism that makes the wildfire programme and the transmission programme share a recovery channel
productsAndServices.positioning: A transmission owner in two regional processes and none in its largest rate-base state — the mirror image of AEP, whose entire strategy is a transmission franchise monetized across four planning processes. Xcel's 765 kV work is bid competitively rather than held as an incumbent franchise.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Regional planning processes in MISO and SPP; state certificates in Colorado.
targetSegments: Regional load in MISO and SPP
Generation interconnection for the resource-plan build
productsAndServices.roadmap: The Crawfish Draw to Phantom 765 kV line at approximately $2B and additional 2025 SPP portfolio lines are competitive bids in the line-of-sight plan; MISO Tranche 2.2 is dated 2030 and beyond.

productsAndServices.name: Wildfire mitigation as a capital programme
productsAndServices.description: Approximately $5B of the $60B base capital plan is wildfire mitigation — a line item of a size that has no counterpart in the other three utility dossiers in this file. The Colorado Public Utilities Commission unanimously approved the 2025–2027 Wildfire Mitigation Plan, and the company states it has public-facing mitigation plans in every state with approved plans in Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. The programme is the company's operational answer to a liability the same commission will also decide how to price.
highlights: The stated strategy: deploying weather stations and AI cameras, building meteorology, fire science and risk-modelling capability, hardening the system with enhanced powerline safety settings and system segmentation to reduce the scope of public safety power shutoffs, materially increasing shutoff drills, and investigating every ignition

Recovery runs through four named channels: Colorado's Transmission Cost Adjustment for qualifying projects; a planned 2029 Colorado securitization, whose effect is already visible in the capital plan's own footnotes as a reduction in 2029 distribution spend; base rate cases, with the 2025 Colorado electric case naming $65M of liability insurance as a driver; and deferral orders for excess liability insurance premiums in Colorado, Wisconsin and New Mexico, with Texas pending

Insurance economics moved sharply: through the third quarter of 2024 the company carried approximately $600M of excess liability coverage including $520M of wildfire coverage at a premium of about $40M a year; from October 2024 it carries $450M of total coverage at a premium of approximately $130M, renewed in October 2025 at about $135M — roughly a threefold premium increase for less coverage

The company's own reading of the legal landscape: neither inverse condemnation nor strict liability has been applied in utility wildfire cases in any of its states, and supportive legislation passed in 2025 in Texas, North Dakota and South Dakota — but not in Colorado, which is not checked under 'Legislation Passed' on the company's own framework grid
productsAndServices.positioning: The only utility in this corpus running wildfire mitigation as a multi-billion-dollar capital programme with its own securitization plan. It is simultaneously the company's largest operational risk and, because the spending enters rate base and riders, a material component of its rate-base growth.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Commission-approved mitigation plans recovered through riders, base rates, deferrals and a planned securitization.
targetSegments: All customers in the high-risk service territories, principally Colorado and the Texas and New Mexico panhandle
productsAndServices.roadmap: The 2025–2027 Colorado plan is in execution; a planned 2029 Colorado securitization is embedded in the capital plan; the company states it continues to explore legislative structures in the states that have not passed them.

productsAndServices.name: Natural gas distribution and the customer programmes
productsAndServices.description: Xcel serves 2.2 million natural gas customers with 2,100 miles of transmission and 38,000 miles of distribution pipeline and 53.3 Bcf of storage, generating $2,452M of gas revenue in 2025 on deliveries of 400,982 thousand MMBtu. Gas carries $3,720M of the 2026–2030 capital plan. Alongside it sit the demand-side programmes: energy efficiency and conservation, electric-vehicle infrastructure with a stated 2035 goal of supporting 1.5 million vehicles, distributed generation interconnection, and a Colorado virtual power plant procurement of up to 125 MW.
highlights: Gas carbon commitments: net-zero greenhouse gas from natural gas use in buildings by 2050 and net-zero methane gas service by 2030
Colorado's gas rate case settled at $123M and a 9.2 percent return in July 2026, with a commission decision expected in the fourth quarter; Minnesota's settled at $38M

Colorado's fuel-cost mechanism under Senate Bill 23-291 took effect for gas in January 2026, sharing 4 percent of the price change against a three-year average and capped at roughly $7M, with an electric version capped near $3M expected during 2026
First-half 2026 weather-normalized firm gas sales fell 1.5 percent system-wide
productsAndServices.positioning: A conventional gas utility attached to an electric business whose growth story it does not share — gas is 25 percent of customers and 6 percent of the capital plan.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Regulated retail gas service under state tariffs.
targetSegments: Residential and commercial gas customers in Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin and the Dakotas
productsAndServices.roadmap: Colorado gas decision expected Q4 2026; the Colorado electric fuel-cost mechanism expected during 2026.

strategyRead: (High confidence) We assess that wildfire is the organizing fact of this company's balance sheet, and that it has been priced rather than resolved. Basis: the Marshall Fire settled at approximately $640M with roughly $350M from insurance and, in the company's own words, 'none from its customers' — leaving about $298M of shareholder charges and the only GAAP-to-ongoing reconciling item of 2025; the Smokehouse Creek complex, which the Texas A&M Forest Service attributed to SPS-owned power lines after wooden poles failed, has produced $404M of settlements against a $525M policy period with approximately $80M of coverage remaining at June 30, 2026, and the company states it 'remains unable to reasonably estimate any additional loss or the upper end of the range'; excess liability insurance now costs roughly $135M a year for $450M of coverage against about $40M for $520M two years earlier; and approximately $5B of the $60B base capital plan is wildfire mitigation, with a planned 2029 Colorado securitization already embedded in the plan's own capital tables. The exposure is bounded by settlements reached, not by a liability regime.

(High confidence) We assess that Xcel has responded to the load-growth problem by contracting its supply chain upstream rather than procuring project by project, and that this is the clearest strategic differentiator in its file. Basis: within one week of February 2026 it signed a strategic alliance with GE Vernova — a reservation agreement for five F-class gas turbines, a capacity reservation for multiple gigawatts of wind turbines, and collaboration on grid equipment including synchronous condensers, later restated as twelve gas combustion-turbine reservations with options into the 2030s — and a memorandum of understanding with a NextEra Energy subsidiary, converted to a joint development agreement in April 2026, to co-develop generation for approximately 2 GW of data-center capacity under a fully regulated ownership structure mixing power purchase agreements, build-own-transfer projects and self-builds. Both were announced before the tariffs that would price the load were approved.

(High confidence) We assess that the Google agreement is a materially different commercial template from anything else in this corpus, and that its significance is the charge rather than the megawatts. Basis: rather than certifying gas plant for a named customer as Entergy does, Xcel filed a 1,900 MW clean-energy package — 1,400 MW of wind, 200 MW of solar and 300 MW of long-duration storage — for approval through a proposed Clean Energy Accelerator Charge, under which 'Google will pay all costs for its new service for the duration of the contract' and the company projects approximately $1.1B of benefits to other Minnesota customers. The storage inside it is a 300 MW, 30 GWh Form Energy iron-air system, a hundred-hour duration procured inside a customer's service agreement rather than through a resource plan. A decision is expected in early 2027.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that the gap between Xcel's contracted and pipeline figures is the widest of the four utilities in this file, and that the company keeps it that way deliberately rather than conservatively. Basis: the same three-tier slide appears unchanged in the Q1 and Q2 2026 decks — approximately 2 GW contracted or under construction, approximately 4 GW contracted by the end of 2027, more than 20 GW of additional pipeline — the contracted block did not grow between April and July 2026, one 200 MW project's online date slipped a year between the two decks, and the fifth project row is redacted in Xcel's own slide. Against AEP's 69 GW of contracted load and Oncor's 298 GW queue, a 2 GW contracted figure held flat for two quarters is either unusual discipline or unusual slowness, and the evidence does not yet separate the two.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that Colorado is simultaneously the company's largest rate base, its widest large-load net and its thinnest regulatory room, and that this combination is the principal near-term risk to the plan. Basis: Colorado is 43 percent of 2025 rate base and earned the lowest return of any operating company at 7.22 percent on a trailing basis; its August 2026 electric order cut the increase to $157M from the $225M the parties had settled and adopted a 13-month average historical test year; Moody's and S&P both carry negative outlooks on the Colorado utility, and Moody's carries one on the parent; the state's proposed large-load tariff sets the lowest threshold of the three at 50 MW with the highest minimum demand charge at 80 percent, and is not decided until early 2027; and the state is not checked under 'Legislation Passed' on the company's own wildfire framework grid, unlike Texas, North Dakota and South Dakota.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that Public Service Company of Colorado's absence from any regional transmission organization is an underappreciated structural feature of this company, and that it changes what can be sold there. Basis: the Form 10-K states the Colorado utility 'is not presently a member of an RTO' while making sales into other regional markets and participating in SPP's Western Energy Imbalance Service. There is therefore no capacity auction setting a price in Colorado, no regional planner allocating its transmission cost, and no independent load forecast to check the utility's own — the commission's approval of a 3 percent compound growth forecast and a 5,400 MW need is the only such finding. Every megawatt of Colorado supply is procured through a state resource-plan solicitation, which makes the commission the effective buyer in the company's largest state.

(Low confidence) We assess that Southwestern Public Service is being positioned as the growth engine and is simultaneously the concentration of the company's unresolved liability, and that the two have not been reconciled in public. Basis: the Texas and New Mexico utility carries the highest rate-base growth rate in the group at approximately 22 percent, $19.0B of five-year capital second only to Minnesota, a build that back-loads hard at roughly 2,490 MW entering service in 2028 and 1,740 MW across 2029–2030, a July 2025 portfolio of 17 projects totalling 5,168 MW nameplate, and a stated resource need of 5,300 to 10,200 MW by 2030 — and it is also the company that owned the poles the state forest service says caused the Smokehouse Creek complex, faces a Texas Attorney General suit filed in December 2025, and has no large-load tariff of its own in either of its states.

policyExposure.regime: Minnesota's super-large-load tariff and the statutory requirement behind it
policyExposure.exposure: The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission ordered NSP-Minnesota to file a proposed tariff for customers with super-large load — largely data centers — by July 15, 2025, and approved the resulting tariff in the second quarter of 2026. Xcel structures the Google agreement 'in accordance with Minnesota's regulatory and legislative requirements for large loads', under which the customer 'will pay all costs for its new service for the duration of the contract'. The tariff is the mechanism by which a 1,900 MW package can be added without the cost falling to other customers, and its approval is what allowed the Google filing to advance to a decision expected in early 2027. Xcel does not cite the underlying statute by bill number in any first-party source reviewed.
policyExposure.mitigation: The company filed the tariff on the commission's schedule and built the Google agreement to sit inside it, with a Clean Energy Accelerator Charge as the recovery vehicle and roughly $1.1 billion of projected benefit to other customers as the public case for approval.

policyExposure.regime: Colorado's proposed large-load tariff, Proceeding No. 26AL-0137E
policyExposure.exposure: Colorado's proposed tariff sets the lowest applicability threshold of the three states at 50 MW and the highest minimum demand charge at 80 percent, and it is not decided until early 2027. Colorado is 43 percent of 2025 rate base and earned the lowest return of any operating company at 7.22 percent on a trailing basis, so the state that most needs a working large-load mechanism is the one that does not yet have one. Until the proceeding concludes, Colorado large-load service is negotiated against a commission that in August 2026 reduced the settled electric increase from $225 million to $157 million and changed the test-year convention.
policyExposure.mitigation: Xcel filed the tariff rather than waiting to be ordered to, and paired it with the NextEra joint development agreement, which names Colorado among the states where co-developed generation would serve large load.

policyExposure.regime: Wildfire liability in Colorado and Texas, and the state legislation Xcel does and does not claim
policyExposure.exposure: Two fires define the exposure. The Marshall Fire settled at approximately $640 million, with roughly $350 million from insurance and, in the company's words, none from customers, leaving about $298 million of shareholder charges and the only GAAP-to-ongoing reconciling item of 2025. The Smokehouse Creek complex, which the Texas A&M Forest Service attributed to Southwestern Public Service-owned power lines after wooden poles failed, has produced $404 million of settlements against a $525 million policy period with approximately $80 million of coverage remaining at June 30, 2026, and the company states it remains unable to reasonably estimate any additional loss or the upper end of the range. Xcel's own wildfire framework credits legislative wins in Texas, North Dakota and South Dakota only; Colorado is not checked under Legislation Passed, and no Colorado utility wildfire-liability statute is named in any source reviewed. Excess liability insurance now costs roughly $135 million a year for $450 million of coverage, against about $40 million for $520 million two years earlier.
policyExposure.mitigation: Approximately $5 billion of the $60 billion base capital plan is wildfire mitigation; the Colorado wildfire mitigation plan for 2025 to 2027 is approved with a transmission cost adjustment and a planned 2029 securitization already embedded in the plan's capital tables; insurance costs are deferred for recovery; and AI-based wildfire detection has been deployed in the Texas Panhandle since December 2024.

policyExposure.regime: Public Law 119-21, the One Big Beautiful Bill, and the clean-energy tax credit wind-down
policyExposure.exposure: The law eliminates production and investment tax credits for wind and solar facilities placed in service after 2027 where construction begins after July 4, 2026, and adds foreign-entity-of-concern rules for projects commencing construction after 2025. Xcel's financing plans depend on tax credit transferability — cash transfers of $652 million in 2025 and $689 million in 2024 — and on federal tax credit carryforwards of $1,474 million at December 31, 2025, with a stated valuation consideration of whether credits are expected to be sold at a discount. Treasury issued beginning-of-construction guidance in August 2025 and initial foreign-entity guidance in February 2026, with more expected through 2026.
policyExposure.mitigation: The company states it does not expect these provisions to affect the 2026 to 2030 base capital plan, 'as steps have been taken to begin construction under the IRS' safe harbor guidance' — the GE Vernova wind capacity reservation is consistent with securing equipment early enough to qualify.

policyExposure.regime: Large-load customer concentration as a named 10-K risk factor
policyExposure.exposure: Xcel added a risk factor stating that growth in large-load customers may increase customer concentration, capital requirements and revenue variability, that additional demand from a limited number of customers may increase credit risk exposure and require incremental infrastructure investment, and that if anticipated load growth does not materialise as expected or regulatory cost allocation mechanisms evolve, results of operations, financial condition or cash flows could be affected. It is now a standing forward-looking-statement factor in every release. The company's own disclosure supports the concern: the contracted block held flat at roughly 2 GW between the Q1 and Q2 2026 decks, one 200 MW project's online date slipped a year between them, and the fifth project row is redacted in Xcel's own slide.
policyExposure.mitigation: The tariffs are the mitigation: minimum demand charges, contract terms and cost-causation provisions in Minnesota, Colorado and Wisconsin are designed so that a customer that does not arrive still pays for what was built. Xcel also holds the contracted figure conservative and reports pipeline separately rather than blending the two.

policyExposure.exposure: The 10-K states that significant events including disallowance of costs, use of historic test years, elimination of riders or interim rates, increasing depreciation lives, lower returns on equity and changes to equity ratios may affect cash flows and credit metrics. Three of those six occurred in Colorado in August 2026 at once: a historic test year was adopted, the increase was cut from the settled amount, and the outcome landed while Moody's carries negative outlooks on both Public Service Company of Colorado and the parent, and S&P carries one on the Colorado utility. The company is funding a $60 billion base plan plus more than $10 billion of line-of-sight capital against that backdrop.
policyExposure.mitigation: Equity has been issued well ahead of need — roughly $1.5 billion in the first quarter of 2026, about half the five-year plan, with 69.7 million forward shares unsettled at June 30, 2026 representing $5.2 billion of minimum proceeds — and liability management has included tender offers for first mortgage bonds.

policyExposure.regime: Resource-plan approval as the procurement gate in a state with no regional transmission organization
policyExposure.exposure: Public Service Company of Colorado 'is not presently a member of an RTO', though it makes sales into other regional markets and participates in the Southwest Power Pool's Western Energy Imbalance Service. There is therefore no capacity auction setting a price in Colorado, no regional planner allocating its transmission cost and no independent load forecast to check the utility's own. Every megawatt of Colorado supply is procured through a state resource-plan solicitation, which makes the commission the effective buyer in the company's largest state. The current cycle is Proceeding No. 24A-0442E; the Phase II competitive solicitation has selected nothing, with bids due in the third quarter of 2026.
policyExposure.mitigation: The company runs procurement through separate near-term and resource-plan tracks so that near-term need can be met while the main solicitation runs, and it secured turbine and wind capacity through the GE Vernova alliance ahead of the solicitations that will use them.

In post since October 2023; interim general counsel January to May 2024
Executive vice president and chief legal and compliance officer, June 2022 to October 2023; executive vice president and general counsel, June 2020 to June 2022
With Xcel Energy since 2015 — a legal career converted into the commercial seat

decisionMakers.name: Scott Sharp
decisionMakers.title: Executive Vice President and Chief Generation Officer
background: One of the two officers who absorbed the chief operations officer role when it was eliminated in May 2025
Holds energy supply and commercial operations, and added oversight of nuclear on promotion
Senior vice president, energy supply and commercial operations, April 2023 to April 2025; vice president, energy supply operations, October 2020 to April 2023
With Xcel Energy since 2014. No company-published headshot exists — his biography page is JavaScript-rendered and he is absent from the newsroom leadership gallery

decisionMakers.name: Michael Lamb
decisionMakers.title: Executive Vice President and Chief Delivery Officer
background: The other half of the split chief operations officer role, and the officer under whom wildfire and the build programme sit together
Scope is electric distribution and transmission, gas distribution and transmission, wildfire risk management, operations process and performance, and the major projects group
Senior vice president, customer delivery, September 2024 to April 2025; distribution and gas, June 2023 to August 2024; transmission, April 2018 to May 2023

With Xcel Energy since 1985 — 41 years, the longest tenure on the executive team. Coordinating officer for the board's operations, nuclear, environmental and safety committee. No company-published headshot exists

decisionMakers.name: Ryan Long
decisionMakers.title: Executive Vice President, Chief Legal and Compliance Officer
background: Took the general counsel seat in June 2025, in the middle of both wildfire liability matters, succeeding Rob Berntsen
Interim president of NSP-Minnesota June to October 2025; president of NSP-Minnesota January 2024 to June 2025 — an operating-company president who moved to legal rather than the reverse
Interim general counsel October 2023 to January 2024; vice president and deputy general counsel from May 2021
Previously a lawyer at Faegre Baker Daniels in Minneapolis and Cravath, Swaine & Moore in New York; serves on the board of the Guthrie Theater. Oversees legal, compliance and federal affairs

decisionMakers.name: Bria Shea
decisionMakers.title: President, Xcel Energy – Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota
background: Named October 2025, succeeding Ryan Long, over the operating company that approved the large-load tariff and signed the Google agreement
Previously regional vice president, planning and policy — led government affairs and regulatory strategy for resource, transmission and distribution planning across the Upper Midwest systems
Joined Xcel Energy in 2008 and held several leadership positions on the regulatory team
The named Xcel spokesperson on the February 2026 Google agreement. BA, Gustavus Adolphus College; law degree, William Mitchell College of Law; board member, Minneapolis Clean Energy Partnership

decisionMakers.name: Robert Kenney
decisionMakers.title: President, Xcel Energy – Colorado
background: Runs Public Service Company of Colorado — 43 percent of 2025 rate base, the lowest trailing earned return in the group at 7.22 percent, and the only operating company in no regional transmission organization
Owns the two 2026 Colorado rate cases, the proposed large-load tariff in Proceeding No. 26AL-0137E and the resource plan in Proceeding No. 24A-0442E
Career detail beyond the title is not published in the first-party sources reviewed

decisionMakers.name: Karl Hoesly
decisionMakers.title: President, Xcel Energy – Wisconsin and Michigan
background: Runs NSP-Wisconsin, the smallest operating company and the one with the highest allowed return at 9.8 percent
Delivered the November 2025 multi-year outcome of roughly $126 million electric and $22 million gas across 2026 and 2027
Career detail beyond the title is not published in the first-party sources reviewed

decisionMakers.name: Alice Jackson
decisionMakers.title: Senior Vice President, System Strategy and Chief Planning Officer
background: The planning-side counterpart to the customer organisation — owns system strategy across the eight states
Listed in Xcel's newsroom leadership gallery; not among the named executive officers in the 10-K
The resource plans in Colorado, Minnesota and the Southwestern Public Service territory all run through this function

decisionMakers.name: Patricia Correa
decisionMakers.title: Senior Vice President and Chief Human Resources Officer
background: In post since February 2022
Previously senior vice president, human resources, at Eaton Corporation, July 2019 to January 2022
Owns a workforce of 11,534 full-time employees at December 2025, about 44 percent of whom are under collective bargaining agreements

decisionMakers.name: Rob Clark
decisionMakers.title: Senior Vice President and Chief Communications Officer
background: Owns external communications through two wildfire liability matters and the Google announcement
Listed in Xcel's newsroom leadership gallery

decisionMakers.name: Amy Schneider
decisionMakers.title: Vice President, Corporate Secretary and Securities
background: Corporate secretary through a period of unusual board turnover — the board moved from 14 members to 12 to 11 between January 2025 and July 2026
Listed in Xcel's newsroom leadership gallery
